issues.legal_issue: A competent civil court may rectify a trust instrument when it fails to express the parties’ real intention because of fraud or mutual mistake.
material_facts: The settlor sought rectification of the written trust deed, alleging that a mutual mistake had caused it to fail to express the intention to create a public charitable trust.
The civil court granted the requested rectification.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to entertain a suit to rectify the trust deed; the Revenue’s challenge to that jurisdiction was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 31 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and 26 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permit rectification of an instrument in writing, including a trust deed, when fraud or mutual mistake prevents it from expressing the parties’ real intention. The Court approved the approach in Jagdamba Charity Trust v. Commissioner of Income-Tax and distinguished Trustees of H.E.H. the Nizam’s Pilgrimage Money Trust v. Commissioner of Wealth-Tax, which concerned a court’s lack of power under a different provision.

predicates.civil_rectification_suit: A party brought a civil proceeding seeking rectification of an instrument.
predicates.written_trust_instrument: The instrument sought to be rectified created or set out the terms of a trust.
predicates.alleged_mutual_mistake: The party seeking rectification alleged that a mutual mistake caused the instrument not to express the parties’ real intention.

issues.definition: When a civil rectification suit concerns a written trust instrument alleged to misstate the parties’ intention because of mutual mistake, the civil court can rectify the instrument.

issues.legal_issue: A tax assessor must consider a trust deed in its rectified form when determining the trust’s tax treatment for an assessment period in which that form applies.
material_facts: A civil court had decreed rectification of the trust deed.
The trust relied on the rectified deed in tax assessment proceedings.
The Revenue argued that the assessor could disregard the decree because the Revenue had not been a party to the rectification proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The assessor could not insist on applying the original deed instead of the rectified deed, but had to interpret the deed as rectified and determine its legal effect.
issues.legal_principle: A rectification decree binds the parties to the instrument and beneficiaries, and the trustees must administer the trust according to the rectified terms. Under the approach approved in Jagdamba Charity Trust v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, an assessor must consider the instrument in the form in which it applies to the relevant assessment period; the assessor may determine what the rectified terms mean for tax purposes but may not simply disregard them.

predicates.income_tax_assessment: A tax authority was determining the tax treatment of a trust for an assessment period.
predicates.civil_rectification_decree: A civil court had issued a decree rectifying the trust instrument.
predicates.rectified_terms_apply_to_assessment: The rectified terms governed the trust during the period being assessed.

issues.definition: In a tax assessment, if a civil court has rectified a trust instrument and the rectified terms apply to the period assessed, the assessor must consider those terms.

issues.legal_issue: A decree rectifying a trust deed is not a judgment in rem, but it is relevant in tax assessment proceedings that put the trust’s entitlement to exemption in issue.
material_facts: The trust relied on a civil court’s decree rectifying its trust deed in proceedings concerning its income-tax exemption.
The Revenue contended that the decree could not be relied on because the Revenue had not been a party to the rectification proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The decree was not a judgment in rem, but it was relevant in the assessment proceedings and had to be considered for its proper evidentiary and legal effect.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 41 and 42 of the Evidence Act, 1872 did not apply to make the rectification decree a judgment in rem or otherwise relevant on those grounds. Section 43 made such a decree relevant where its existence was a fact in issue or relevant under another provision; section 11 made the decree relevant to the issue whether the trust, on the basis of its rectified instrument, qualified for tax exemption.

predicates.income_tax_assessment: A tax authority was determining the tax treatment of a trust.
predicates.trust_exemption_in_issue: The proceeding required a determination of whether the trust’s income qualified for tax exemption.
predicates.civil_rectification_decree: A civil court had issued a decree rectifying the trust instrument.

issues.definition: When a tax assessment puts a trust’s exemption in issue, a civil decree rectifying its deed is relevant but is not a judgment in rem.

issues.legal_issue: A later rectification that substitutes a new trust arrangement operates prospectively rather than changing the trust’s character for earlier assessment periods.
material_facts: A second civil court decree rectified the trust deed and was treated as substituting a new trust arrangement for the earlier one.
The assessee accepted that the second rectification operated prospectively.
issues.conclusion: The second rectification operated prospectively and did not affect the assessment periods preceding it.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the second rectification had no retrospective effect because it effectively created a new trust or substituted a new arrangement for the old one. The Court therefore rejected the High Court’s contrary answer on the issue.

predicates.tax_assessment: A tax authority was determining a trust’s tax treatment for an assessment period.
predicates.later_rectification_decree: A civil court later issued a decree rectifying the trust instrument.
predicates.rectification_substituted_new_arrangemen: The rectification substituted a new trust arrangement for the earlier arrangement.

issues.definition: If a later rectification substitutes a new trust arrangement, it operates prospectively in determining the trust’s tax treatment.

issues.legal_issue: A trust deed creates a public charitable trust when its operative objects benefit a defined public class in need and do not require the trustees to confine benefits to the settlor’s employees.
material_facts: The deed as rectified provided for charitable and public-utility objects, including assistance with housing for workmen in the area who were poor and in need.
It also provided for schools, libraries, hospitals, recreation facilities, and other public-utility works.
The deed did not require the trustees to give benefits only to the settlor’s employees; evidence showed that workers outside the settlor’s group benefited as well.
For later assessment periods, the tribunal had allowed exemption under the applicable provisions, subject to the statutory limit and conditions for the years governed by the later Act.
issues.conclusion: The deed as rectified created a public charitable trust. The trust’s income qualified for exemption for the relevant later assessment periods, subject to the conditions applicable under the governing tax provisions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the charitable-purpose provisions in section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 and sections 2(15) and 11 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. A defined section of the public may be a charitable class, and a discretionary ability to benefit the settlor’s employees does not defeat public character where the deed does not oblige the trustees to prefer them. The Court relied on Trustees of the Charity Fund v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Andhra Chamber of Commerce, Ahmedabad Rana Caste Association v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Abdul Sathar Haji Moosa Sait Dharmastapanam v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income-Tax, Sole Trustee, Loka Sikshana Trust v. Commissioner of Income-Tax, and Yogiraj Charity Trust v. Commissioner of Income-Tax. It also applied the distinction in Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Walchand Diamond Jubilee Trust between discretionary preference and a binding priority for a private group.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and charitable_public_objects and defined_public_class_in_need and no_mandatory_employee_priority

predicates.income_tax_assessment: A tax authority was determining a trust’s entitlement to exemption for its income.
predicates.charitable_public_objects: The trust instrument provided objects directed to charitable purposes or public utility.
predicates.defined_public_class_in_need: The instrument identified a section of the public in need as beneficiaries.
predicates.no_mandatory_employee_priority: The instrument did not require the trustees to confine benefits or give binding priority to the settlor’s employees.

issues.definition: If an assessed trust has charitable public objects for a defined class in need and does not mandate priority for the settlor’s employees, it qualifies for charitable tax exemption subject to applicable conditions.

issues.legal_issue: A trust deed does not establish a wholly public charitable trust when it obliges trustees to provide benefits in particular to the settlor’s employees, even if it also refers to workmen generally.
material_facts: The 1945 rectification referred to housing for workmen generally but required housing in particular for the settlor’s workmen, staff, other employees, and employees of allied concerns.
The deed did not limit that employee group to people who were poor or in need, and the group could include affluent employees.
The trust also had other charitable objects, but the employee-benefit obligation formed part of the deed’s objects.
issues.conclusion: The deed as rectified in 1945 did not hold the trust property wholly for charitable purposes and did not qualify the trust for exemption for the earlier assessment periods.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(3)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 required the property to be held wholly for religious or charitable purposes. A public class may include a needy class of workmen, but a binding obligation to benefit a defined group of the settlor’s employees, including persons not necessarily poor, makes the supposed public benefit illusory. The Court approved the test in Commissioner of Income-Tax v. Walchand Diamond Jubilee Trust, which distinguishes a discretionary preference from an obligatory priority, and agreed with the relevant reasoning in J.K. Hosiery Factory v. Commissioner of Income Tax and Mercantile Bank of India (Agency) Ltd. v. Commissioner of Income-Tax.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment and deed_benefits_workmen_generally and mandatory_employee_priority and employee_class_not_limited_to_needy

predicates.income_tax_assessment: A tax authority was determining whether a trust qualified for exemption for its income.
predicates.deed_benefits_workmen_generally: The trust instrument referred to benefits for workmen generally.
predicates.mandatory_employee_priority: The trust instrument required trustees to provide benefits in particular to the settlor’s employees or employees of associated concerns.
predicates.employee_class_not_limited_to_needy: The employee beneficiaries were not restricted to people who were poor or in need.

issues.definition: If a trust deed refers to workmen generally but mandates benefits for an employee class not limited to people in need, the trust is not wholly charitable.
